subject: Cognitive Science
title: Statistical Learning in Infants
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Statistical Learning in Infants.

hook.text: Play 'bidakupadotigolabubidaku' to an 8-month-old for two minutes. They'll find the hidden word boundaries.

buildup.text: Jenny Saffran showed that infants track transitional probabilities—which syllables tend to follow which.

discovery.text: Within 'bidaku,' 'bi' always precedes 'da.' But across word boundaries, transitions are unpredictable.

twist.text: Babies detect these statistical patterns within minutes—without feedback, without reward, without instruction.

climax.text: This statistical learning mechanism works for music, visual patterns, and even social sequences—not just language.

punchline.text: Before they speak, babies are running statistics.

quiz.question: How do infants find word boundaries in speech?

details.summary: Saffran showed that eight-month-old infants track statistical regularities in speech to find word boundaries. In a continuous stream of syllables, infants detect which syllables co-occur reliably and use transitional probabilities to segment words.
details.whyItMatters: Statistical learning explains how infants begin cracking the language code before they understand any words. It is a general-purpose mechanism that also applies to visual and musical patterns.
takeaways: Infants detect syllable co-occurrence patterns at eight months
Transitional probabilities help segment continuous speech
Statistical learning operates across sensory domains

faq.question: How was statistical learning in infants demonstrated?
faq.answer: Saffran exposed eight-month-olds to a continuous stream of artificial syllables with no pauses. After two minutes of exposure, infants could distinguish three-syllable words from non-words based solely on transitional probabilities between syllables.

faq.question: Is statistical learning specific to language?
faq.answer: No. The same mechanism operates in visual pattern learning, music perception, and action sequences. Infants and adults track statistical regularities across all sensory domains. This generality suggests statistical learning is a fundamental cognitive mechanism, not a language-specific module.
